title: The Man Nobody Talks About Who May Have Changed Your Eternity
paragraphs:
The Man Nobody Talks About Who May Have Changed Your Eternity
The Lesson I Learned From Epaphras Never Stopping His Prayers
Most Christians dream of doing something great for God.
We imagine standing on stages, leading movements, writing books, planting churches, changing nations, influencing millions, leaving a legacy that outlives us.
Yet one of the most powerful men in the New Testament never wrote a Gospel.
He never performed a recorded miracle.
He never became one of the Twelve.
He never preached a sermon that was preserved in Scripture.
In fact, many believers have read the Bible for years and barely remember his name.
His name was Epaphras.
And the older I get, the more convinced I become that heaven may reveal him as one of the most influential believers who ever lived.
Not because of what he built.
Not because of what he accomplished.
But because he never stopped praying.
That sounds ordinary until you realize that most of us stop.
We stop when answers delay.
We stop when circumstances worsen.
We stop when discouragement grows louder than faith.
We stop when people disappoint us.
We stop when our own hearts grow tired.
But Epaphras didn't.
And that realization hit me harder than I expected.
The Apostle Paul wrote something remarkable about him in Colossians 4:12.
"Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God."
The Greek text uses the phrase:
"ἀγωνιζόμενος ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"
(agōnizomenos hyper hymōn)
The word "ἀγωνιζόμενος" (agōnizomenos) is where we get the idea behind the English word "agonize."
It describes intense effort.
A struggle.
A fight.
An athletic contest.
A battle requiring endurance.
Paul was not describing a man casually mentioning names during prayer.
He was describing a warrior.
A man entering spiritual battle for people he loved.
A man who refused to surrender.
A man whose knees carried burdens that were not even his own.
And suddenly prayer looks very different.
Because prayer is not merely informing God about our problems.
Prayer is participation in God's purposes.
Prayer is warfare.
Prayer is surrender.
Prayer is dependence.
Prayer is love expressed through persistence.
Epaphras understood something many of us have forgotten.
Real love keeps showing up.
Even when nobody notices.
Even when nobody applauds.
Even when there is no visible reward.
Maybe that's why his story convicts me.
Because I often want visible results.
I want measurable progress.
I want confirmation that my efforts matter.
Yet Epaphras reminds us that some of the greatest victories happen where nobody can see them.
Inside prayer closets.
Inside sleepless nights.
Inside whispered cries.
Inside tears nobody else knows about.
And isn't that where many of us live right now?
Maybe you're praying for a prodigal son.
Maybe you're praying for a struggling marriage.
Maybe you're praying for healing.
Maybe you're praying for freedom from addiction.
Maybe you're praying for someone who has walked away from Christ.
Maybe you're praying for your own heart because you're exhausted from pretending you're okay.
You have prayed.
And prayed.
And prayed.
Yet nothing seems to change.
At least not yet.
The temptation is to quit.
The temptation is to assume heaven is silent.
The temptation is to believe your prayers are accomplishing nothing.
But Scripture repeatedly tells a different story.
James 5:16 says:
"The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working."
The Greek reads:
"πολὺ ἰσχύει δέησις δικαίου ἐνεργουμένη"
(polý ischýei déēsis dikaíou energoumenē)
Literally emphasizing that the prayer of the righteous is actively effective.
Not eventually effective.
Not potentially effective.
Actively effective.
Even when we cannot see what God is doing.
And perhaps that is one of the hardest lessons faith teaches us.
God is working in places our eyes cannot reach.
He is moving through conversations we never hear.
He is softening hearts we think are impossible.
He is orchestrating circumstances we cannot understand.
He is writing chapters we cannot yet read.
After all, the entire Gospel is built upon people assuming God was doing nothing.
The disciples thought everything was over on Friday.
The cross looked like failure.
The blood looked like defeat.
The silence looked permanent.
The grave looked final.
Yet what appeared to be the greatest scandal in human history became the greatest display of grace the world would ever witness.
That is the story of Christianity.
That is the story of redemption.
That is the story of Jesus.
The Hebrew word often translated grace is "חֵן" (chen), carrying the idea of favor that is freely given.
The Greek New Testament word is "χάρις" (charis), meaning grace, favor, kindness, and undeserved blessing.
Grace is God doing for us what we could never do for ourselves.
Grace is God moving when we have nothing left.
Grace is God continuing His work when our strength is gone.
And nowhere is that more visible than at the cross.
When Jesus cried:
"Τετέλεσται"
(Tetelestai)
"It is finished."
He was not declaring defeat.
He was announcing victory.
The debt was paid.
The sacrifice was accepted.
The way home was opened.
The scandal of the cross became the doorway of grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites failures.
He rewrites regrets.
He rewrites broken stories.
He rewrites prodigals.
He rewrites addictions.
He rewrites shame.
He rewrites the future of anyone willing to surrender.
And perhaps that is why Epaphras kept praying.
Because he believed God was still writing.
He believed grace was still moving.
He believed Christ was still transforming lives.
He believed no situation was beyond redemption.
He believed God could do more than human effort ever could.
The truth is, some of you are reading this because someone became an Epaphras for you.
A praying mother.
A praying father.
A praying grandparent.
A praying spouse.
A praying friend.
A praying pastor.
Someone fought battles for your soul when you didn't even know they were fighting.
Someone refused to quit when you were running from God.
Someone believed Jesus could rewrite your story before you believed it yourself.
And perhaps now God is calling you to become that person for someone else.
To stop measuring prayer by immediate results.
To stop measuring faithfulness by visible outcomes.
To stop quitting simply because answers have not arrived on your timetable.
Because heaven never wastes a prayer offered in faith.
Not one tear.
Not one cry.
Not one burden.
Not one whispered plea.
Not one desperate midnight conversation with God.
Your honesty may become the encouragement another believer desperately needed today.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't ignore that feeling. Sometimes God uses a simple act of obedience to place hope exactly where it is needed most.
One day heaven may reveal that the prayers you thought accomplished nothing were the very prayers God used to change everything.
